question.problem: Given the equation ${y}^{″}-10{y}^{′}+25y=0$ for $y=y(x),$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?
question.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-10\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+25{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -5)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and so $\lambda =5$ is a repeated root of the auxiliary equation.

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{5x}$ and $x{e}^{5x}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only ${e}^{5x}-5{e}^{x}$ is not a solution.
